- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

start_coordinate.description: (x, y): The starting coordinates for `left_click_drag`.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract the visible text of the Browser pane's page (article/main content first, falls back to body innerText).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description: Action to perform (only `javascript_exec` is supported).

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. Return values are serialized as JSON.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__navigate
tools.description: Navigate the Browser pane to a URL, or go "back"/"forward" in history. If the Browser pane isn't open yet, this opens it at the URL (no dev server needed).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

force.description: If the page shows a "Leave site?" dialog because of unsaved changes, discard those changes and navigate anyway. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_list
tools.description: List servers started with preview_start. Returns serverIds for use with other preview_* tools.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_logs
tools.description: Get server stdout/stderr output. Use to check for build errors, verify server behavior, or read debug output. Use 'level' to filter to errors only, or 'search' to filter for specific text. Use after preview_start.

level.description: Filter by level: 'all' (default) shows all output, 'error' shows only lines containing error/exception/failed/fatal

search.description: Filter to lines containing this text (e.g., '[DEBUG]', 'POST /api')

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start

name.description: Server name from .claude/launch.json.

url.description: URL to open in the Browser pane without a dev server (instead of starting one by `name`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_stop
tools.description: Stop a server started with preview_start.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_console_messages
tools.description: Get console output (log, info, warn, error, debug) from the Browser pane.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

limit.description: Max entries to return (default: 50, max: 200).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_network_requests
tools.description: List network requests, or fetch a specific response body by `requestId`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

urlPattern.description: Substring filter on the request URL as listed (auth values show as REDACTED).

requestId.description: If provided, returns the response body for this request instead of listing.

limit.description: Max entries to return when listing (default: 50).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_page
tools.description: Read the current page in the Browser pane as a YAML-style accessibility tree. Each interactive element is tagged `[ref_N]` for use with `computer`/`form_input`/`find`. Prefer this over screenshot for verifying text and structure. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default; if it exceeds the limit it is truncated with a note — pass a larger max_chars, or use ref_id/depth to focus.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

filter.description: 'interactive' returns only clickable/typable elements; 'all' (default) returns the full tree.

ref_id.description: Restrict the tree to descendants of this `ref_N` (from a previous read_page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_close
tools.description: Close one Browser pane tab. Closing the last tab closes the Browser pane itself (reopen it with `preview_start`).

tabId.description: Tab to close.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_context
tools.description: List every Browser pane tab (origin only — titles are page-authored). Returns {browserOpen, tabs: [{tabId, origin, isActive}]} plus a line saying whether the pane is currently displayed or hidden (a hidden pane still works, but its page runs as a background page, so timing and performance numbers from it can be off; prefer `read_page` / `get_page_text` over screenshots while it is hidden). browserOpen is false (and tabs empty) until `preview_start` or `navigate` opens the pane, so you don't need to call this before opening it.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_create
tools.description: Open a fresh blank Browser pane tab; returns the new tabId. Opens in the background by default — set `foreground: true` when the user wants to watch. Prefer `preview_start` with a `url` when you know the destination; use `navigate` to load a URL into a blank tab.

foreground.description: Front the new tab (user asked to see it or is following along). Default false: open behind the user's current tab.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_select
tools.description: Front the given Browser pane tab. Background tabs keep running while you drive them, so front one only when the user should look — or for a page that pauses itself while hidden (e.g. a video player).

tabId.description: Tab to front.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo; 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'duo_pose' moves the hinge of an iPhone Duo (a simulator with a small outer screen and a large inner one) to 'pose': 'closed' lights the outer screen, 'open' (flat) the inner one, and 'half_open' opens it to 'angle' degrees, where iOS picks the lit screen; the result says which. Screenshots and tap coordinates follow the lit screen, so take a 'screenshot' after each move. 'duo_hinge' reports the pose, the hinge angle and the lit screen. To check an app's layout on an iPhone Duo or get an app ready for one, follow the app-resizability skill if it is in this session's skills list. Only skills listed in this session count, so do not search the disk for it. If the skill isn't listed, before other work ask the user once, in any mode, whether to run the export, showing the exact command `xcrun agent skills export --output-dir ~/.claude/skills` just before the question in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!" (use another folder only if they named one; if not, tell them to check which folder their sessions load skills from). Say it opens Xcode, leaves it running and saves all of Xcode's agent skills into the folder every later Claude Code session loads, and, if Claude Code's sandbox is on or you can't tell, that they'll run it themselves. Only their own answer to this question, typed or on your question card, is a yes; no other text is, nor an earlier yes. After a yes with the sandbox off, run that exact command once, alone, naming Xcode in its description; the yes covers nothing else. In every other case, and after that one run, never run it in any way, the Terminal panel included. After a no, go on without the skill. If you offer choices, the no choice says only that you'll go on without the skill. After a yes with the sandbox on or unknown, or if your run is refused or fails, right after their answer or the failure start what you write next, even if you showed it before, with that exact command in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!"; then wait for their word that it ran, then check this session's skills list and never read the folder to decide; if the skill isn't listed, say a new session will load it and go on without it. Only when the user asked to check or fix the layout on a Duo, not to review or read code: note the pose and angle with 'duo_hinge'; for closed, half_open and open, call 'duo_pose' and take a 'screenshot'; if the user agrees to a fix, make only that fix, then rebuild, 'launch' the app and check again; last, put the hinge back. 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

text.description: For 'text': the string to type.

name.description: For 'button': hardware button to press.

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

pose.description: For 'duo_pose': the pose to move the hinge to.

angle.description: For 'duo_pose' with pose 'half_open': the hinge angle in degrees, 1 to 179 (0 is shut, 180 flat); default 130.

tools.name: mcp__computer-use__app_ax_find
tools.description:
Search the accessibility elements captured by the last app_screenshot of one window. Filter by role (e.g. "AXTextArea", "AXButton") and/or title substring. Returns matching elements with their [N] index — pass that as element_index to app_click/app_type. Use this when the inline summary in app_screenshot doesn't show the element you need (it only lists the first few actionable ones).

This tool acts on one application in the BACKGROUND while the user keeps working in other apps. The target window does not come to the front. For the menu bar use app_menu. `app` says which application a call acts on. To act in another granted application, call the app_* tools with that application; no release is needed in between. When you come back to an application, take a fresh app_screenshot first: a coordinate or an element_index points at a place in the capture it came from, not at an element.

tools.name: mcp__computer-use__app_zoom
tools.description:
Get a closer look at part of a window you have already captured with app_screenshot: returns just that region, at the display's full pixel density so small text and fine detail are legible. Reading aid only — it does not replace your app_screenshot: coordinates for app_click and every other app_* tool keep referring to the app_screenshot, never to the zoomed image, and the zoomed image carries no element summary.

This tool acts on one application in the BACKGROUND while the user keeps working in other apps. The target window does not come to the front. For the menu bar use app_menu. `app` says which application a call acts on. To act in another granted application, call the app_* tools with that application; no release is needed in between. When you come back to an application, take a fresh app_screenshot first: a coordinate or an element_index points at a place in the capture it came from, not at an element.

Pass a different id to switch windows — there is no separate switch-window tool; targeting is per-call via this parameter.

Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

tools.name: mcp__computer-use__computer_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of actions in ONE tool call. Each individual tool call requires a model→API round trip (seconds); batching a predictable sequence eliminates all but one. Use this whenever you can predict the outcome of several actions ahead — e.g. click a field, type into it, press Return. Actions execute sequentially and stop on the first error. The frontmost application must be in the session allowlist at the time of this call, or this tool returns an error and does nothing. The frontmost check runs before EACH action inside the batch — if an action opens a non-allowed app, the next action's gate fires and the batch stops there. Screenshot and zoom actions are allowed and their images are returned interleaved with the per-action outputs. Coordinates you write in THIS batch — clicks AND zoom regions — always refer to the full-screen screenshot taken BEFORE this call, never to a zoom and never to a mid-batch screenshot. After the batch returns, the most recent full screenshot it produced becomes the new coordinate reference for your next call. In this session the tools that each carry out one of this tool's actions (left_click, type, key, scroll, left_click_drag, screenshot, etc.) are not available on their own: a single action is a one-item batch. The app_* tools (app_screenshot, app_click, app_type, app_key, app_batch, etc.) act on granted applications without taking over the screen.

tools.name: mcp__computer-use__teach_batch
tools.description: Queue multiple teach steps in one tool call. Parallels computer_batch: N steps → one model↔API round trip instead of N. Each step still shows a tooltip and waits for the user's Next click, but YOU aren't waiting for a round trip between steps. Returns {exited:true, stepsCompleted:N} if the user clicks Exit — do NOT call again after that; {stepsCompleted, stepFailed, ...} if an action errors mid-batch; otherwise {stepsCompleted, results:[...]} plus a final screenshot. tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.

The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__app_click

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__app_key
entries.description:

Use those two keys only while such a box is being edited: in a document body (Pages, TextEdit) they select the WHOLE document, and in a list or on a selected table cell they do other things. Press escape once; another with nothing left to cancel only plays the Mac's alert sound.

entries.description:

entries.name: mcp__computer-use__computer_batch
entries.description: Execute a sequence of actions in ONE tool call. Each individual tool call requires a model→API round trip (seconds); batching a predictable sequence eliminates all but one. Use this whenever you can predict the outcome of several actions ahead — e.g. click a field, type into it, press Return. Actions execute sequentially and stop on the first error. The frontmost application must be in the session allowlist at the time of this call, or this tool returns an error and does nothing. The frontmost check runs before EACH action inside the batch — if an action opens a non-allowed app, the next action's gate fires and the batch stops there. Screenshot and zoom actions are allowed and their images are returned interleaved with the per-action outputs. Coordinates you write in THIS batch — clicks AND zoom regions — always refer to the full-screen screenshot taken BEFORE this call, never to a zoom and never to a mid-batch screenshot. After the batch returns, the most recent full screenshot it produced becomes the new coordinate reference for your next call. In this session the tools that each carry out one of this tool's actions (left_click, type, key, scroll, left_click_drag, screenshot, etc.) are not available on their own: a single action is a one-item batch. The app_* tools (app_screenshot, app_click, app_type, app_key, app_batch, etc.) act on granted applications without taking over the screen.

action.description: The action to perform.

coordinate.description: (x, y) for click/mouse_move/scroll/left_click_drag end point.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs the clang-tidy check that gates pull requests (.github/workflows/clang_tidy.yml)
# on your branch, so its findings match what CI reports. Linux and macOS.
#
#   scripts/run_clang_tidy.sh            check your changes against OrcaSlicer's main
#   scripts/run_clang_tidy.sh --fix      also add the missing includes it names
#
# It configures a separate build directory (build-tidy) without the precompiled
# header, uses the clang-tidy on your system or installs the pinned one into a
# virtual environment inside it, and runs scripts/clang_tidy_diff.py the way CI
# does. Uncommitted changes are checked too.
set -euo pipefail
usage() {
    cat <<'EOF'
Usage: scripts/run_clang_tidy.sh [options]
  -b, --base REV       revision to compare against (default: main of the remote that
                       points at OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer, else origin/main)
      --no-fetch       do not fetch that remote's main first
  -B, --build-dir DIR  build directory for the compile database (default: build-tidy)
  -d, --deps-dir DIR   dependency build directory (default: deps/build on Linux,
                       deps/build/<arch> on macOS)
  -j, --jobs N         parallel clang-tidy runs (default: all cores)
      --fix            apply clang-tidy's fixes (adds the missing includes)
  -y, --yes            install missing tools without asking; another clang-tidy
                       version found on the system is then not offered
  -h, --help           show this help
EOF
}
ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)
cd "$ROOT"

content.text:
The JusPrin app now sends its error reports straight to your Sentry project `jusprin-app`, and the server endpoint that used to forward them is removed. The app change is on branch `claude/errors-straight-to-sentry` in `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/errors-straight-to-sentry`. The server change sits in the shared tsd-enterprise checkout. Neither is committed or pushed. I didn't touch the IP address setting.

**What changed in the app**
- **Sending code:** the app has no Sentry library, so I reused the HTTP client and JSON library it already uses. Adding Sentry's own C++ library would mean building a new dependency on three platforms just to make one upload. The new code is in `Support/SentryEnvelope.{hpp,cpp}`, and the sending call is in `ErrorReport.cpp`.
- **What the event carries:** what the server used to add, namely the release (the app's version line), a tag for what the app was doing and a tag for the system. The app sets the grouping itself, as what it was doing plus the error text with request ids removed. A grouping rule on the Sentry project can't remove part of a message, and it would live outside the code and its tests.
- **Network addresses:** Sentry would fill in the sender's address if an event claimed to come from a browser, which the server's version did whenever a page stack was attached. The app now always says "native" and tells Sentry never to fill in the address. I checked that against Sentry's processing code; it can't be tested without sending to the real Sentry.
- **Where the key lives:** the release workflow reads it from a GitHub secret called `JUSPRIN_SENTRY_DSN` and compiles it in, so the public repository never names the Sentry host. A build without the key, such as a developer build or a fork, sends nothing and writes one log line. Anyone can still read the key out of a shipped app, but that's unavoidable for direct sending, and the key can only create new events.

**What changed on the server:** the endpoint, its setting, its test file and the docker-compose line are removed. The stand-in Sentry those tests used moved into the gateway failure tests, which still need it. The production-check skill now says the app reports to `jusprin-app`. The repository's `CLAUDE.md` never described the endpoint, so it's unchanged.

**What I tested**
- **Unit tests:** 6 new tests. The grouping and "native" checks fail when I break those parts and pass again once restored. All 188 tests in the app's suite pass, and the include check that CI runs passes.
- **Server tests:** all 317 pass. The local server now answers 404 at the old address.
- **Live runs:** a scratch copy of the app with its own data folder, and a stand-in on this Mac playing both the JusPrin server and Sentry:
  - Automatic reports on, start report failing: exactly one event, with release, tags and grouping.
  - Reports off, same failure: nothing sent.
  - Automatic reports on, a page error: one event. The grouping left out the request id and the message kept it.
  - Reports off, a page error: the dialog opened and nothing was sent for four minutes. Pressing "Report to JusPrin team" sent exactly one event.
- **Key in the build:** a fake key given to CMake ended up in the compiled code intact.

**Checks you asked for**
- **Released versions:** none calls the old endpoint. JusPrin 2.0.0 predates it. But a 2.0.1 release is being prepared, uncommitted, in another worktree (`release-2.0.1`), on top of the commit that still sends to the server. If 2.0.1 ships from there, its reports go nowhere. It needs this branch first.
- **Public internet:** your Sentry accepts events from it. The two phone-app projects on it receive events daily.
- **Dialog and privacy wording:** the dialog's sentences stay true. The privacy policy only says people may send "us" problem reports, which still holds because your Sentry is self-hosted. One sentence becomes inaccurate, in Preferences › Updates under the automatic-reports switch: "JusPrin's server sees your IP address, as with any web page." Reports now go to the Sentry server, not the JusPrin server. I haven't reworded it.

**Still open**
- **GitHub secret:** someone with admin access has to add `JUSPRIN_SENTRY_DSN` to the repository. I can't read or set secrets. Until it exists, release and nightly builds send no reports.
- **Other platforms:** Windows and Linux aren't built or tested here, and neither is the workflow reading the secret on GitHub.

Details and evidence paths are in `errors-straight-to-sentry.md` in the shared notes folder.

<cross-session-message from="local_b262996b-705a-4553-8f66-281a6e117a77" from-name="btw: We want the Sentry server to capture as much info as possi…">
Kenneth decided the app should use Sentry's own libraries in place of your hand-written upload: the C++ one (sentry-native) in the app and the browser one in the app's pages.

His words, 2026-11-17: "We want the Sentry server to capture as much info as possible so that we can do production troubleshooting." I then asked him "Should I tell that session to switch to Sentry's own libraries?", with my pick stated as "the official libraries, with nothing sent until the person agrees". He answered: "Yes, switch". I am the session that wrote your brief, in a fork; I relay his words and add no permission of my own.

Why the hand-written upload falls short of his goal: it sends the error sentence, the version, two labels and a text stack from pages only. It sends no C++ stack, nothing about what led up to the failure, nothing about the machine, and nothing at all when the app crashes.

What to build
1. Replace `Support/SentryEnvelope.{hpp,cpp}` and the sending call in `Support/ErrorReport.cpp` with sentry-native. Use what the library offers before writing code of your own: stacks, the list of loaded modules, machine and system details, the trail of events before a failure, attachments, crash capture.
2. In the pages (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI` and `HomeUI`), use Sentry's browser library so a page failure arrives with a real stack and the page's own trail. Decide whether the page sends by itself or hands the event to the app, and say why.
3. Keep what you already built that still applies: the release, the two labels, grouping that ignores request ids, and the Sentry key coming from the `JUSPRIN_SENTRY_DSN` secret so the public repository names no production host.
4. C++ stacks are readable in Sentry only if each release's debug files are uploaded to it. Work out what the release workflow needs for that and tell Kenneth what he has to set up.

What stays as decided
- Nothing is sent before the person presses "Report to JusPrin team" or has automatic reports on. sentry-native has a setting that holds everything back until the person agrees (`require_user_consent`); check how it behaves, do not take my word for it.
- A crash cannot ask first. Find out, by running it, whether the library can keep a crash report and send it once the person agrees on the next start. Two projects describe this differently, so I do not know. If "nothing sent until the person agrees" cannot be met for crashes, bring Kenneth that as a "Decision needed" paragraph with the options and what each costs.
- The report dialog promises what a report contains (no chat messages, no project names, no account). The libraries collect things by themselves, such as addresses of requests and file paths. List what each library would send by default, turn off what breaks a promise, and tell Kenneth about any sentence in the dialog, Preferences or the privacy policy that becomes untrue. Do not reword those sentences yourself.

Rules for the work
- sentry-native is a new dependency in the dependency build, which is OrcaSlicer-owned. Read `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md` before editing anything outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`.
- It must build on Windows, macOS and Linux. Only macOS builds on this Mac; say plainly what is untested.
- Send nothing to a real Sentry project unless Kenneth says so. Use the stand-in.
- Shared Mac: check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja` before building, use `-- -j4`, one build per build directory.
- Commit nothing unless Kenneth asks. No secrets in messages, notes or commit messages.

Two things I found reading your uncommitted code, which Kenneth has not answered on, so they are information and not instructions: no real Sentry server has ever accepted an upload from this work, and a release built without the key, or with a mistyped one, would send no reports and say so only in a log line.

Done looks like: with the scratch app and the stand-in, a C++ failure and a page failure each produce one event carrying a stack and the trail before it; with reports off, nothing is sent; you show what happens on a crash; the app's tests pass. Report to Kenneth in plain language, with what you tested and what is still open.

1	# Fork stewardship
2	
3	**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-dev`.
4	
5	JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.
6	
7	One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**
8	
9	- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
10	- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
11	- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.
12	
13	Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.
14	
15	## The ten principles
16	
17	### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much
18	
19	**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.
20	
21	**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.
22	
23	**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?
24	
25	**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.
26	
27	### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge
28	
29	**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.
30	
31	**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.
32	
33	**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?
34	
35	**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.
36	
37	### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it
38	
39	**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.
40	
41	**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.
42	
43	**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?
44	
45	**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.
46	
47	### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism
48	
49	**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.
50	
51	**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.
52	
53	**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?
54	
55	**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.
56	
57	### 5. One seam beats many touch points
58	
59	**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.
60	
61	**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.
62	
63	**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?
64	
65	**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.
66	
67	### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict
68	
69	**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.
70	
71	**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.
72	
73	**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.
74	
75	**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.
76	
77	### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly
78	
79	**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.
80	
81	**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.
82	
83	**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?
84	
85	**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.
86	
87	### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went
88	
89	**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.
90	
91	**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.
92	
93	**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?
94	
95	**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.
96	
97	### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it
98	
99	**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.
100	
101	**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.
102	
103	**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?
104	
105	**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.
106	
107	### 10. Take each upstream release by merging from the release we last took
108	
109	**Rule.** Take a new upstream release with a merge whose base is the upstream release the fork last took. Never run a plain `git merge` of upstream, and never rewrite the fork's history to take a release.
110	
111	**Mechanism.** The fork follows upstream's release branches, and each release branch splits off upstream's development line on its own. A plain merge picks the common ancestor itself, a development-line commit from before both release branches. Its conflict list is then everything that differs between the two release branches: vendor profiles, translations, CI files, none of it ours. Naming the last release we took as the base limits the merge to the fork's own changes. That gives the same conflicts a replay would hit, resolved once, with no commits rewritten, so branches in progress merge forward without a rebase. Measured on 2026-11-07, going from v2.4.2 to v2.5.0: 22 conflicted files either way, and a branch in progress merged into the trial result with no conflicts.
112	
113	**How.** In a worktree on a new branch from `jusprin-dev`, the development branch:
114	
115	```bash
116	git rev-parse <new release>^{commit} > "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/MERGE_HEAD"
117	git merge-recursive <last release taken> -- HEAD <new release>
118	```
119	
120	Resolve the conflicts, then `git commit`. A later patch release on the same release branch, such as 2.5.1 after 2.5.0, needs no override: a plain `git merge` finds the right base.
121	
122	**The test.** Is the merge base the release we last took, and not a commit on upstream's development line?
123	
124	**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main` or `git merge v2.5.0` with no base given. Each produces thousands of conflicts in files JusPrin never edited.
125	
126	## Before you finish
127	
128	A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:
129	
130	1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against the newest upstream release, with the release the fork last took as the base (rule 10), and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.
131	
132	   ```bash
133	   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<last release taken> <newest upstream release> HEAD
134	   ```
135	
136	   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.
137	
138	2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.
139	
140	3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.
141	
142	An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.
143	
144	## This fork's terrain
145	
146	Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.
147	
148	`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.
149	
150	Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.
151	
152	`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
153	upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
154	updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
155	or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
156	error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
157	strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
158	controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
159	print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
160	into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
161	19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
162	needed edits across eight upstream files.
163	
164	The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
165	after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
166	Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
167	correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
168	Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
169	fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
170	Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
171	no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
172	replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
173	addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
174	`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
175	on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
176	must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.
177	
178	Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
179	screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
180	availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
181	selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
182	Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
183	page, silently.
184	
185	Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
186	function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
187	sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
188	`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
189	and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
190	without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
191	owned by Plater's event handler.
192	
193	Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against the newest upstream release, with the release the fork last took as the base (rule 10), and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<last release taken> <newest upstream release> HEAD
   ```

   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.

2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.

3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

## This fork's terrain

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.

Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.

`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
needed edits across eight upstream files.

The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.

Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
page, silently.

Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
owned by Plater's event handler.

Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

# usage: python3 -I sentry_standin.py <port> <out-dir>
# A local stand-in for Sentry: answers every POST with 200 and saves each
# request as <out-dir>/<n>.json (path, headers) and <out-dir>/<n>.body.
import json, os, sys, itertools
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
port, out = int(sys.argv[1]), sys.argv[2]
os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)
counter = itertools.count(1)

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def _answer(self):
        n = next(counter)
        length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0)
        body = self.rfile.read(length) if length else b""
        if self.headers.get("Transfer-Encoding", "").lower() == "chunked":
            chunks = []
            while True:
                size = int(self.rfile.readline().strip(), 16)
                if size == 0:
                    self.rfile.readline(); break
                chunks.append(self.rfile.read(size)); self.rfile.readline()
            body = b"".join(chunks)
        with open(f"{out}/{n}.json", "w") as f:
            json.dump({"method": self.command, "path": self.path, "headers": dict(self.headers.items()), "length": len(body)}, f)
        with open(f"{out}/{n}.body", "wb") as f:
            f.write(body)
        data = b'{"id":"00000000000000000000000000000000"}'
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)
    do_GET = do_POST = do_PUT = _answer
    def log_message(self, *a): pass

ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), Handler).serve_forever()

# usage: python3 -I sentry_standin.py <port> <out-dir>
# A local stand-in for Sentry: answers every POST with 200 and saves each
# request as <out-dir>/<n>.json (path, headers) and <out-dir>/<n>.body.
import json, os, sys, itertools
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
port, out = int(sys.argv[1]), sys.argv[2]
os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)
counter = itertools.count(1)

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def _answer(self):
        n = next(counter)
        length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0)
        body = self.rfile.read(length) if length else b""
        if self.headers.get("Transfer-Encoding", "").lower() == "chunked":
            chunks = []
            while True:
                size = int(self.rfile.readline().strip(), 16)
                if size == 0:
                    self.rfile.readline(); break
                chunks.append(self.rfile.read(size)); self.rfile.readline()
            body = b"".join(chunks)
        with open(f"{out}/{n}.json", "w") as f:
            json.dump({"method": self.command, "path": self.path, "headers": dict(self.headers.items()), "length": len(body)}, f)
        with open(f"{out}/{n}.body", "wb") as f:
            f.write(body)
        data = b'{"id":"00000000000000000000000000000000"}'
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)
    do_GET = do_POST = do_PUT = _answer
    def log_message(self, *a): pass

ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), Handler).serve_forever()
PY

# Fork-owned targets that must exist after the OrcaSlicer target is defined.
# src/CMakeLists.txt reaches this file with a single add_subdirectory; add new
# fork targets here, not there.
add_subdirectory(Mcp/Bridge)
# Bridge exports the AppImage packaging hook one scope up. This file is now
# that scope; forward it to src/ where build_linux_image.sh.in is configured.
set(SLIC3R_PACKAGE_EXTRA_SCRIPT "${SLIC3R_PACKAGE_EXTRA_SCRIPT}" PARENT_SCOPE)
add_subdirectory(Web)
    target_link_libraries(jusprin_mcp_bridge_core PUBLIC ws2_32)
endif()

add_executable(jusprin-mcp main.cpp)
set_target_properties(jusprin-mcp PROPERTIES MACOSX_BUNDLE FALSE
    RUNTIME_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY "$<TARGET_FILE_DIR:OrcaSlicer>")
target_link_libraries(jusprin-mcp PRIVATE jusprin_mcp_bridge_core)
if(WIN32)
    target_link_libraries(jusprin-mcp PRIVATE shell32) # CommandLineToArgvW, for the wide command line
endif()
add_dependencies(OrcaSlicer jusprin-mcp)
if(NOT APPLE)
    if(WIN32)
        install(TARGETS jusprin-mcp RUNTIME DESTINATION ".")
    else()
        install(TARGETS jusprin-mcp RUNTIME DESTINATION "${CMAKE_INSTALL_BINDIR}")
        set(SLIC3R_PACKAGE_EXTRA_SCRIPT "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/package_linux.sh" PARENT_SCOPE)
    endif()
endif()
endif()
