tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

start_coordinate.description: (x, y): The starting coordinates for `left_click_drag`.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

content.content:
# Test suite rules

Rules for writing tests under `tests/`. [CATCH2.md](CATCH2.md) is the Catch2 reference. Building and running the suites is covered on the wiki, at <https://www.orcaslicer.com/wiki/developer_reference/how_to_test.html>.

## The suites

- `libslic3r`: the core library. Geometry, meshes, file formats, config and presets, Clipper, algorithms, data structures.
- `fff_print`: the FFF slicing pipeline, from a `Model` plus config through `Print` and `PrintObject` to emitted G-code.
- `sla_print`: SLA support-tree and pad geometry, support-point generation, raycast.
- `libnest2d`: 2D nesting and packing.
- `slic3rutils`: the Python plugin system and its slicing-pipeline bindings.
- `filament_group`: filament-to-extruder grouping, checked against golden files.
- `cli`: end-to-end runs of the built `orca-slicer` binary, Linux only. These tests carry the `RequiresApp` label, which the CI unit-test job excludes because it receives only `build/tests`; run them with `ctest --test-dir build/tests -C Release -L RequiresApp`.

## Building and running

Tests are off by default, so the build has to be told to include them.

- Windows: `build_win.bat -ds --run-tests`, which builds the dependencies and the tests and runs them (`-l -x` for the clang-cl and Ninja build CI uses)
- macOS: `./build_release_macos.sh -s -a arm64 -T`, which builds and runs them
- Linux: `./build_linux.sh -t`, then `ctest --test-dir build/tests -C Release`

Rebuild a single suite with `cmake --build build --config Release --target <suite>_tests`. Visual Studio, Xcode and the Ninja Multi-Config generator that `build_linux.sh` uses are all multi-configuration, so `ctest` needs `-C` on every platform; without it, tests registered with plain `add_test()` lose their labels and report "Not Run".

## Where a test goes

- Pick the suite by the production code the test exercises, not by how the test is written.
- A property of a class that holds with no `Print` involved belongs in `libslic3r`. Behavior that depends on print settings, or produces or consumes G-code or slicing state, belongs in `fff_print`.
- One file per subsystem, named `test_<subsystem>.cpp`. It owns every test for that subsystem, whether the test reads in-memory state or generated output.
- When you add a file, list it in that suite's `CMakeLists.txt` in the same change.

## Use the existing helpers

Check these before writing your own setup or output-parsing code.

- `tests/test_utils.hpp` is shared by every suite. `load_model()` loads a mesh from `tests/data/`, and `ScopedTemporaryFile` gives a temp path that removes itself.
- `fff_print/test_helpers.hpp` builds and slices a `Print` and parses the emitted G-code. Read it before writing an fff_print test rather than assembling a `Print` by hand.
- The other suites have their own: `sla_print/sla_test_utils.hpp`, `libnest2d/libnest2d_test_utils.hpp`, `slic3rutils/plugin_test_utils.hpp`, `filament_group/fg_test_utils.hpp`. `libslic3r` has none and uses the shared header.
- Test data lives in `tests/data/` and is reached through the `TEST_DATA_DIR` define. Wrap it in `std::string(...)` before joining a path onto it.

## Writing the test

- Name the test case as a plain behavioral sentence in the present tense. No `Subsystem:` prefix.
- Tag it with the subsystem it covers, matching the file, in PascalCase. That tag is what people filter on, so every test needs one.
- Add further tags where they help: a narrower one to slice a large file (`[Rotcalip]`, `[Placer]`), a shared one for something spanning files (`[Python]`, `[H2C]`, `[Regression]`), or `[NotWorking]` / `[.]` to disable or hide a test. Say why in a comment if you disable or hide.
- Prefer a flat `TEST_CASE` per behavior, with `GENERATE` for parameterized cases. Reserve `SCENARIO` / `GIVEN` / `WHEN` / `THEN` for genuine shared setup that branches into a few close variations.
- Set the config keys your test depends on, and derive the expected values from what you set. A 20mm cube sliced at `layer_height` 2 is 10 layers, and the test should state both parts. If a number in your assertion comes from a key you never set, the test is also testing that default.
- Assert the defining property, not an incidental value. "Skirt present" or "at least 2 brim loops" survives a refactor; exact coordinates and byte counts do not.
- Name a regression test for the behavior it protects, never for an issue or PR number.
- When asserting on G-code, match the meaningful token such as `; skirt` rather than whole lines, whitespace or comment wording. Depend on ordering only when ordering is the contract.

## Catch2 rules that cause real breakage

- Never reuse a `SECTION` name inside a loop. Use `DYNAMIC_SECTION` so each iteration is unique.
- Never assert from a spawned thread. Catch2 assertions are not thread-safe. Collect results in the thread and assert on the main thread.
- Never combine conditions with `&&` or `||` inside one assertion. Split them so Catch2 can print both operands on failure.

193 agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md
# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-dev`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

### 10. Take each upstream release by merging from the release we last took

**Rule.** Take a new upstream release with a merge whose base is the upstream release the fork last took. Never run a plain `git merge` of upstream, and never rewrite the fork's history to take a release.

**Mechanism.** The fork follows upstream's release branches, and each release branch splits off upstream's development line on its own. A plain merge picks the common ancestor itself, a development-line commit from before both release branches. Its conflict list is then everything that differs between the two release branches: vendor profiles, translations, CI files, none of it ours. Naming the last release we took as the base limits the merge to the fork's own changes. That gives the same conflicts a replay would hit, resolved once, with no commits rewritten, so branches in progress merge forward without a rebase. Measured on 2026-11-07, going from v2.4.2 to v2.5.0: 22 conflicted files either way, and a branch in progress merged into the trial result with no conflicts.

**How.** In a worktree on a new branch from `jusprin-dev`, the development branch:

```bash
git rev-parse <new release>^{commit} > "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/MERGE_HEAD"
git merge-recursive <last release taken> -- HEAD <new release>
```

Resolve the conflicts, then `git commit`. A later patch release on the same release branch, such as 2.5.1 after 2.5.0, needs no override: a plain `git merge` finds the right base.

**The test.** Is the merge base the release we last took, and not a commit on upstream's development line?

**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main` or `git merge v2.5.0` with no base given. Each produces thousands of conflicts in files JusPrin never edited.

## Before you finish

A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against the newest upstream release, with the release the fork last took as the base (rule 10), and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<last release taken> <newest upstream release> HEAD
   ```

# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-dev`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

#!/bin/zsh
# usage: run-case.sh <case> <launch-status> <on|off> <page:normal|throws> <seconds>
# Runs the scratch copy of the worktree's app once, with its own data folder
# (seeded from the seed run, automatic reports on or off), against the local
# stand-in for JusPrin's server and Sentry, for <seconds>, then stops that
# app only. Prints what the stand-in received.
C=$1; ST=$2; REP=$3; PAGE=$4; SECS=$5
L=/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/75a11bff-4206-4fd9-a7c4-4494377a5bf7/scratchpad/live
APP=$L/JusPrinTest.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer
PORT=8761; PAGEPORT=8762
D=$L/$C; rm -rf $D; mkdir -p $D
if [ "$C" != seed ]; then
  cp -R $L/${SEED_FROM:-seed}/data $D/data; rm -rf $D/data/log
  python3 -I - "$D/data/JusPrin2.conf" "$REP" <<'PY'
import json, sys
path, rep = sys.argv[1:]
text = open(path).read()
data = json.loads(text[:text.rfind("}") + 1])
data.setdefault("app", {})["jusprin_report_errors_automatically"] = "true" if rep == "on" else "false"
open(path, "w").write(json.dumps(data, indent=4))
PY
else
  mkdir -p $D/data
fi
: > $D/received.jsonl
python3 -I $L/standin.py $PORT $ST $D/received.jsonl & rpid=$!
penv=()
if [ "$PAGE" = throws ]; then
  (cd $L/page && python3 -I -m http.server $PAGEPORT --bind 127.0.0.1 > $D/page-server.log 2>&1) & ppid=$!
  penv=(JUSPRIN_HOME_DEV_URL=http://127.0.0.1:$PAGEPORT/${PAGEFILE:-index.html})
fi
[ -n "$FILEURL" ] && penv=(JUSPRIN_HOME_DEV_URL=$FILEURL)
sleep 1
env JUSPRIN_SERVER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:$PORT JUSPRIN_SENTRY_DSN=http://standinkey@127.0.0.1:$PORT/16 $penv $APP --datadir $D/data > $D/stdout.txt 2>&1 & apid=$!
echo $apid > $D/app.pid
if [ -n "$CRASH_AT" ]; then
  # A crash: the signal the kernel sends a process that touched bad memory.
  sleep $CRASH_AT; kill -SEGV $apid; echo "sent SIGSEGV at ${CRASH_AT}s" > $D/crash.txt
  sleep $((SECS - CRASH_AT))
else
  sleep $SECS
fi
kill $apid 2>/dev/null; sleep 3; kill -9 $apid 2>/dev/null
# This app copy's crash handler only, never another app's.
pkill -f "$L/JusPrinTest.app/Contents/MacOS/crashpad_handler" 2>/dev/null
kill $rpid 2>/dev/null; [ -n "$ppid" ] && pkill -P $ppid 2>/dev/null; [ -n "$ppid" ] && kill $ppid 2>/dev/null
echo "== $C: stand-in received"
python3 -I $L/analyze.py $D/received.jsonl "$HOME"
echo "== $C: app log"
grep -h -i "start report\|Unexpected error\|error report" $D/data/log/*.log* 2>/dev/null | cut -c1-300 | head -20

#!/bin/zsh
# usage: run-case.sh <case> <launch-status> <on|off> <page:normal|throws> <seconds>
# Runs the scratch copy of the worktree's app once, with its own data folder
# (seeded from the seed run, automatic reports on or off), against the local
# stand-in for JusPrin's server and Sentry, for <seconds>, then stops that
# app only. Prints what the stand-in received.
C=$1; ST=$2; REP=$3; PAGE=$4; SECS=$5
L=/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/75a11bff-4206-4fd9-a7c4-4494377a5bf7/scratchpad/live
APP=$L/JusPrinTest.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer
PORT=8761; PAGEPORT=8762
D=$L/$C; rm -rf $D; mkdir -p $D
if [ "$C" != seed ]; then
  cp -R $L/${SEED_FROM:-seed}/data $D/data; rm -rf $D/data/log
  python3 -I - "$D/data/JusPrin2.conf" "$REP" <<'PY'
import json, sys
path, rep = sys.argv[1:]
text = open(path).read()
data = json.loads(text[:text.rfind("}") + 1])
data.setdefault("app", {})["jusprin_report_errors_automatically"] = "true" if rep == "on" else "false"
open(path, "w").write(json.dumps(data, indent=4))
PY
else
  mkdir -p $D/data
fi
: > $D/received.jsonl
python3 -I $L/standin.py $PORT $ST $D/received.jsonl & rpid=$!
penv=()
if [ "$PAGE" = throws ]; then
  (cd $L/page && python3 -I -m http.server $PAGEPORT --bind 127.0.0.1 > $D/page-server.log 2>&1) & ppid=$!
  penv=(JUSPRIN_HOME_DEV_URL=http://127.0.0.1:$PAGEPORT/${PAGEFILE:-index.html})
fi
[ -n "$FILEURL" ] && penv=(JUSPRIN_HOME_DEV_URL=$FILEURL)
sleep 1
env JUSPRIN_SERVER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:$PORT JUSPRIN_SENTRY_DSN=http://standinkey@127.0.0.1:$PORT/16 $penv $APP --datadir $D/data > $D/stdout.txt 2>&1 & apid=$!
echo $apid > $D/app.pid
if [ -n "$CRASH_AT" ]; then
  # A crash: the signal the kernel sends a process that touched bad memory.
  sleep $CRASH_AT; kill -SEGV $apid; echo "sent SIGSEGV at ${CRASH_AT}s" > $D/crash.txt
  sleep $((SECS - CRASH_AT))
else
  sleep $SECS
fi
kill $apid 2>/dev/null; sleep 3; kill -9 $apid 2>/dev/null
# This app copy's crash handler only, never another app's.
pkill -f "$L/JusPrinTest.app/Contents/MacOS/crashpad_handler" 2>/dev/null
kill $rpid 2>/dev/null; [ -n "$ppid" ] && pkill -P $ppid 2>/dev/null; [ -n "$ppid" ] && kill $ppid 2>/dev/null
echo "== $C: stand-in received"
python3 -I $L/analyze.py $D/received.jsonl "$HOME"
echo "== $C: app log"
grep -h -i "start report\|Unexpected error\|error report" $D/data/log/*.log* 2>/dev/null | cut -c1-300 | head -20

## Pages on a custom URL scheme (2026-11-17, prototype, uncommitted)

Why: WKWebView gives a file:// page only "Script error." (no file, line, stack) for an uncaught error, and Sentry's browser SDK drops that, so errors thrown from React rendering or from app-delivered messages never reached Sentry on macOS.

What changed (worktree errors-straight-to-sentry, nothing committed):
- New Support/PageFiles.{hpp,cpp}: page_file(root, path), the file under resources/jusprin a jusprin:/// path names; refuses "", ".", "..", backslashes, folders, missing files. Unit tests: tests/jusprin/test_page_files.cpp (3 cases).
- New Support/PageScheme.{hpp,cpp}: page_url("home"/"agent") gives jusprin:///<page>/index.html on macOS and the file:// address elsewhere; page_handlers() gives a wxWebViewHandler for "jusprin" on macOS, nothing elsewhere.
- HomeWebView.cpp and AgentWebView.cpp use page_url() and pass page_handlers() to CreateWebView.
- Orca-owned Widgets/WebView.{hpp,cpp}: one neutral seam, an overload CreateWebView(parent, url, handlers). The old two-argument function forwards to it with no handlers. Handlers are registered before Create on WebKit (macOS, Linux) and after Create on Edge, where wx needs them. No upstream line deleted; the old signature line stays as the forwarding function.
- WebShared/errorReports.ts: comment only.

Checked:
- Swift WKWebView harness: same thrown error gives "Script error." under file:// and full message/file/line/stack under a custom scheme. Custom-scheme page: isSecureContext true, localStorage works, http:// image (printer camera) loads; fetch to http:// fails (neither page uses fetch).
- Live scratch app, Home page with one added error thrown 6 s after load from a timer Sentry does not wrap: file:// run sent nothing; jusprin:/// run sent the event with frame app:///home/index.html line 77 col 88, function homeTrialThrow, dist "local", breadcrumbs showing both Home and the AI page did their hello handshake.
- jusprin_tests 195 cases pass; clang-tidy passes on 27 changed files.
- Rebase simulation (base v2.5.0): against v2.5.1 (eef7710cb1) and upstream/main (07f38df2a4), WebView.cpp/.hpp merge cleanly; the only conflicts (OrcaSlicer.cpp, ProjectStrategy.hpp, Plater.cpp/.hpp) are the same with or without this change. Upstream has not touched WebView.cpp/.hpp since v2.5.0.

Not checked / open:
- Dropping a file on a spot the page does not handle: the app relies on the web view starting a file:// navigation, which it vetoes and opens. Whether WKWebView starts that navigation from a jusprin: page is untested (needs a real drag).

- Visible effect: on macOS, page errors that used to vanish now reach report_unexpected_error, so the person sees the generic "Something went wrong on our side" message for them.
EOF
echo ok

content.text:
On macOS, uncaught errors in the Home and AI pages now reach Sentry in full. Both pages now load from `jusprin:///home/index.html` and `jusprin:///agent/index.html` instead of a `file://` address. Under `file://`, Mac's web view gives only "Script error." for these errors, and Sentry drops that. Nothing is committed.

**What I changed** (all in the `errors-straight-to-sentry` worktree)
- **A file lookup.** `Support/PageFiles` finds the file a `jusprin:///` address names inside `resources/jusprin`. It refuses `..`, `.`, empty path parts, backslashes, folders and missing files.
- **The page address and its handler.** `Support/PageScheme` gives each page's address: `jusprin:///` on macOS, and the old `file://` address on Windows and Linux. It also gives the handler that serves those files.
- **The two callers.** `HomeWebView.cpp` and `AgentWebView.cpp` use that address and pass the handler on.
- **One seam in Orca's `Widgets/WebView`.** There is a new `CreateWebView(parent, url, handlers)`. The old two-argument version forwards to it with no handlers. No upstream line is deleted.

**What I tested**
- **Same error, both addresses.** In the scratch app I added one error to the Home page, thrown 6 seconds after it loads:
  - Over `file://`, nothing reached the stand-in for Sentry.
  - Over `jusprin:///`, the full error arrived: the message, the function `homeTrialThrow`, and the frame `app:///home/index.html` at line 77, column 88.
  - The event's history shows both Home and the AI page finished their handshake with the app.
- **What still works.** In a small test harness, a custom-scheme page counts as a secure page, page storage works, and the printer camera picture (`http://`) still loads.
- **Unit tests.** All 195 JusPrin unit tests pass, including 3 new ones for the file lookup.
- **Include check.** The include check CI runs passes on the 27 changed files.
- **Rebase simulation**, from OrcaSlicer 2.5.0 to 2.5.1 (`eef7710cb1`) and to upstream `main` (`07f38df2a4`):
  - The two `WebView` files merge cleanly.
  - The four files that conflict (`OrcaSlicer.cpp`, `ProjectStrategy.hpp`, `Plater.cpp`, `Plater.hpp`) conflict the same way without my change.

**What the person now sees.** On Mac, page errors that used to vanish now show the generic "Something went wrong on our side" message with a way to report it. That is what the error-handling rules ask for every unexpected error, but people will see it more often.

**Still open**
- **Dropping a file onto a page.** If the page doesn't catch the drop, the app opens the file only when the web view starts loading the file's `file://` address. Whether Mac's web view still does that from a `jusprin:///` page is untested; it needs a real mouse drag.
- **Windows and Linux.** They still load from `file://`. It's untested whether their web views also hide these errors.
  - Linux can't just reuse the Mac code. There, wx registers a scheme once for the whole app and ties it to the first web view that registered it, so closing that view would leave the scheme pointing at freed memory.

Details are in `errors-straight-to-sentry.md` in the shared notes folder, under "Pages on a custom URL scheme".

content.text:
I deleted both trims, as you said. Error reports now carry the error text and its location exactly as the app found them. The app no longer swaps your home folder for `~`, and no longer cuts fields at 500, 8,000 or 32,000 bytes. Nothing is committed or pushed.

**What changed:** only `make_error_report` in `Support/ErrorReport.cpp`, which now passes the three fields through untouched.
- No test checked either trim, so no test needed changing.
- The sentences in the report dialog and in Preferences are as they were.
- Nothing was done on the Sentry server.
- I left one cut in place: tags are still cut at 200 bytes, because Sentry itself refuses longer tag values.

**Testing:**
- The JusPrin unit tests (195 cases) and the AI-bridge tests (612 cases) pass. Neither includes the report code, so they only show nothing else broke.
- To test the change itself, I ran the scratch copy of the app with a Home page that throws a 9,051-byte error containing the home folder path. It reached the local stand-in for Sentry whole, with the full path and no `~`.

**How long the three stack items take, and which could wait:** all three are already built and tested on Mac (uncommitted), so the code costs no more time. What's left in each:

- **Stacks that show where an error was thrown.** This is app code only and is finished. It could ship alone. Without it, reports still arrive, but their stack shows where the error was reported rather than where it was thrown.
- **File and line numbers for Mac and Linux crashes and errors.** This adds steps to the release workflow and scripts. What's left is one real release run on GitHub, which took about 1 hour 50 minutes on the last two successful runs, and one real report checked in Sentry.
  - Releases already upload debug files to Sentry. With this change, a release also fails if Sentry doesn't end up holding file-and-line information for the build.
  - The Linux steps are untested.
- **Page source maps** (so page errors name the page's source files and lines). These are also new release-workflow steps, and what's left is the same release run and check.
  - It could follow later. Without it, page errors still arrive, but point into the built page rather than the source files.

Leaving out either of the last two makes nothing worse than today. Each is checked only in that release run, and the run needs your yes because it uploads to the real Sentry project.

The Mac change to load Home and the AI page from `jusprin:///`, done earlier today, is separate from all three. It is what lets uncaught page errors reach Sentry at all on Mac.

The program throws `std::invalid_argument` from its own function and catches it, then calls `std::stoi("not a number")`, which throws inside the system's C++ library, and inside that catch calls `current_exception_throw_stack()`.
   Result: before any app throw, `stoi` gives 0 frames, as designed. After the app throw, `stoi` gives 3 frames, and they are the earlier app throw's (`app_throws`, `main`, `start`). `std::string("abc").at(10)` does the same. `std::filesystem::file_size` on a missing file gave 0 frames in that run.
   Why: the lookup matches on the thrown object's address alone, and the C++ runtime hands a freed exception's address to the next one. An unrecorded throw at a reused address finds the old record.
   Why it matters: the report then names a throw site that had nothing to do with the failure, which is worse than naming the handler. Throws inside the system library are common ones: `std::stoi` and its family, `std::filesystem`, some `std::string` checks.

An unrecorded throw must fall back to the reporting code's stack, never to another throw's. Check the Windows path for the same mistake: there the latest throw on the thread is used without comparing the object.

   `sentry_page_maps.sh upload` fails when Sentry already holds a different `index.html` for the same commit, on the assumption that every platform builds the same page.    Check it before changing anything: convert the embedded files to CRLF in a scratch copy, build the page, and compare the output. If it differs, make the pages build the same on every platform or make the upload handle one page per platform, whichever is smaller; say which you chose and why. If it does not differ, say what you ran.

Limits as before: commit and push nothing, send nothing to the real Sentry project, change no production system, no filtering code in the app, one build per build directory with `-- -j4`. I cannot approve anything for Kenneth beyond his words already quoted to you.

content.content:
I can't show the Windows and POSIX sections verbatim because they're too long to quote within the 125-character limit per quote. Here is a concise summary of how each path works.

**Windows (`_MSC_VER` / MinGW)**

- **Capture:** A vectored exception handler, installed at static initialization, watches for MSVC C++ exception records. When it sees a throw that isn't a rethrow, it grows a thread-local array of entries and records the thrown object's address as the key. It then writes a 4096-byte stack dump, skipping 4 frames, into that entry.
- **Rethrow detection:** A throw is treated as a rethrow if its object address is zero or matches the currently active C++ exception. Rethrows don't create new dumps.
- **Lookup:** `boost_stacktrace_impl_current_exception_stacktrace` gets the active exception record from the VC runtime, then searches the array from newest to oldest for a matching object address. It returns that dump, or null if none matches.
- **Ownership:** The dumps and array are freed in the thread-local data's destructor. There is no refcount handling, no `exception_ptr` handling, and no `__cxa_*` hook on this path.

**POSIX (non-MSVC)**

- **Capture hook:** `__cxa_allocate_exception` is overridden and forwards to the real function via `dlsym(RTLD_NEXT)`. When capture is enabled, it rounds the thrown size up to max alignment, allocates an extra 4096 bytes, and writes a stack dump (skipping 1 frame) directly after the thrown object.
- **Storage with the libstdc++/GCC ABI:** The dump pointer is stored in the reserved padding of the exception header. The code asserts that this padding was zeroed beforehand.
- **Storage with libc++:** The runtime is detected through a weak symbol. Unless `BOOST_STACKTRACE_ALWAYS_STORE_IN_PADDING` is set, the dump pointer is stored in a mutex-guarded map keyed by the exception object's address.
- **Lookup:** `current_exception_stacktrace` returns null if capture is disabled. Otherwise it calls `std::current_exception()` and extracts the raw exception object pointer from it. That pointer is the key, either into the map or into the padding. Matching is by object identity, so it refers to the exception actually being handled.
- **Refcounting (libc++ only):** `__cxa_decrement_exception_refcount` is overridden. When the refcount is 1, the map entry is erased before the original function runs. The code notes a race that can cause a false positive or a leak.
- **Leak guard:** Concurrent throws on libc++ may leak. The program aborts with a warning unless `BOOST_STACKTRACE_LIBCXX_RUNTIME_MAY_CAUSE_MEMORY_LEAK=1` is set, or the library was built with the matching macro defined.
- **`__cxa_begin_catch`:** No hook for it appears in this code.
- **Debug guard:** In non-NDEBUG builds, a thread-local counter guards `__cxa_allocate_exception` against runaway recursion.
- **Cleanup check:** `assert_no_pending_traces` asserts that the libc++ map is empty.

content.content:
# Set the default behavior, in case people don't have core.autocrlf set.
* text=auto

# Shell scripts are run by Git Bash on Windows CI, which cannot read a script
# with CRLF line endings: it fails on the first line. Windows checkouts default
# to core.autocrlf=true, so keep these LF whatever the platform.
*.sh text eol=lf

# Batch files are read by cmd.exe, which tracks a byte offset into the file to
# resume after `call :label`. With LF endings that offset can land wrong and the
# label lookup fails, so keep these CRLF whatever the platform.
*.bat text eol=crlf

# OCCT BRep fixtures, kept byte for byte as OCCT wrote them.
*.brep -text
----
   2 author EpiphanyPrinting	summary Adds resonance avoidance ported from qidi slicer (#9403)
   5 author ExPikaPaka	summary Cache system presets to eliminate startup and wizard load times (#14217)
   5 author Kris Austin	summary build: add build_win.bat, a Windows build script for deps, slicer and toolchain setup (#15436)
   3 author Kris Austin	summary build: update OCCT to 8.0.1 (faster STEP and Design tab, Windows STEP crash fix) (#16089)

## Two bugs from the checking fork fixed (2026-11-17, uncommitted)

1. Wrong throw stack after an address is reused (reproduced with the fork's scratch program and with a new test, failing first).
   - Cause: records matched by thrown-object address; libc++ gives a freed exception's memory to the next one, and throws inside libc++.dylib (std::stoi, std::string::at) are not recorded on macOS.
   - Fix (ThrowStack.cpp, POSIX): the app also overrides __cxa_begin_catch; the first time app code catches an exception, the newest record of its address takes an std::exception_ptr to it, so the address cannot be reused while the record exists. A lookup returns a stack only from a record that holds the exception being handled; otherwise failure_stack falls back to the reporting code's stack. Records live in a leaked ring of 32, so held exceptions are not destroyed at exit; the oldest one is released outside the lock.
   - Remaining case that can still name the wrong throw: a recorded exception caught and freed only by code outside the app (e.g. libc++'s istream swallowing an app streambuf's exception), then an unrecorded throw at the same address caught by the app.
   - Effect: an exception the app caught stays alive until 32 newer throws, so its destructor runs later.
   - Windows: the handler now keeps a per-thread ring keyed by thrown object, skips rethrows (no object, or the object being handled), and a report finds its exception through vcruntime's __current_exception(), as Boost.Stacktrace does. Not compiled or run: no Windows build here.
   - Tests: "A throw the app's code does not make never gets an earlier throw's stack" (failed before, passes after); "An exception kept and thrown again later still has its throw's stack" (macOS/Linux only).
2. Page-map upload would fail on Windows (confirmed by measurement).
   - Real git checkouts of the page folders with core.autocrlf=true vs false: 306 files get CRLF; the AI page and both source maps differ (Home page itself same, its template was already LF).
   - Fix: .gitattributes in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin (AgentUI, HomeUI, WebShared, Localization), resources/jusprin and docs/guide: text=auto eol=lf. No upstream file changed. With them, the autocrlf=true checkout builds both pages and maps byte for byte the same as the LF one.
- All suites pass: jusprin_tests 197, agent_bridge_tests 612, AgentUI 834, HomeUI 168; clang-tidy passes; live scratch app still sends the start-report 500 event and runs normally.
EOF
echo ok

I fixed both problems. A report no longer gets an earlier throw's stack, and the pages now build byte for byte the same with Windows line endings. Everything is tested on Mac, except the Windows C++ change, which I couldn't compile here. Nothing is committed.

**1. Wrong throw stack**

- **Reproduced:** with your program and with a new test in `tests/jusprin/test_throw_stack.cpp`. The test failed on the old code: `std::stoi` and `std::string::at` errors got the earlier app throw's frames.
- **Fix on macOS and Linux:** the app now also has its own `__cxa_begin_catch`, which runs at every catch in the app's code. The first time the app catches a recorded exception, the record keeps a hold on that exception. While it holds it, the runtime can't give its address to another exception. A lookup accepts only a record holding the exception being handled; anything else falls back to the reporting code's stack.
  - The test now passes.
  - Your program now shows 0 frames for `stoi` and `string::at`, while the app's own throw keeps its 3.
  - A second new test checks that an exception stored and rethrown later still finds its own throw. That is the path the AI page's host uses.
- **Cost:** an exception the app caught stays alive until 32 newer throws have been recorded, so its destructor runs later than before.
- **One case can still name the wrong throw:**
  1. The app throws an exception that only code outside the app ever catches, for example the C++ library's stream code swallowing a failure from one of the app's streams.
  2. That exception is freed.
  3. A throw the app can't see then reuses its address, and the app catches it.

  I found no way to close this on macOS without reaching into the C++ runtime's private data.
- **Windows:** the old code took the latest throw on the thread without comparing anything. It now keeps the thread's recent throws keyed by the thrown object, skips rethrows, and finds the exception being handled through `__current_exception()`, as Boost.Stacktrace does on Windows. This part has not been compiled or run.

**2. Page-map step on Windows**

- **Measured:** I checked the page folders out twice with git, once with `core.autocrlf=true` as the Windows runner does, and once with it off.
  - With it on, 306 files got CRLF.
  - The AI page came out different, and so did both pages' source maps. The upload compares the maps too, so both pages would have failed.
- **Fix:** make the pages build the same everywhere, which was smaller than keeping one map per platform. New `.gitattributes` files in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin` (covering `AgentUI`, `HomeUI`, `WebShared` and `Localization`), `resources/jusprin` and `docs/guide` keep those files LF on every checkout. No upstream file changed.
- **Result:** with the rules, the Windows-style checkout builds both pages and both maps byte for byte the same as the Mac and Linux one.

**Checks run:**
- The JusPrin unit tests (197 cases), the AI-bridge tests (612) and the AI page (834) and Home page (168) tests pass.
- The include check passes.
- The scratch copy of the app ran normally, and its start-report HTTP 500 still arrived as an error report.

Sources:
- [Boost.Stacktrace from_exception.cpp](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boostorg/stacktrace/develop/src/from_exception.cpp)
- [Wine mailing list on `__current_exception`](https://list.winehq.org/archives/list/wine-gitlab@list.winehq.org/message/FVSRN5O4R24JROB2LNBSMDF7DVS7FZBD)
- [ReactOS excpt.h](https://doxygen.reactos.org/d5/d85/include_2vcruntime_2excpt_8h_source.html)
